BILL NUMBER:S4851

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the agriculture and markets law, in
relation to agricultural districts law improvements; and the real
property tax law, in relation to tax exemptions for certain structures
on agricultural and horticultural lands; and to repeal certain
provisions of the agriculture and markets law relating to agricultural
districts

Purpose of the Bill:

The purpose of this bill is to streamline the process for the
creation, review and consolidation of agricultural districts and
provide a property tax exemption for certain impermanent structures
and buildings used exclusively in the raising and production for sale
of agricultural or horticultural commodities.

Summary of Provisions:

Section 1 amends Agriculture and Markets Law (AML) § 301(3) to remove
from the definition of "farm woodland" the requirement that woodland
products grown on the land be produced for sale.

Section 2 amends AML § 301(11) to make conforming amendments to
reflect amendments made by Section 4 of the bill.

Section 3 amends AML § 301(12) to make conforming amendments to
reflect amendments made by Section 16 of the bill.

Section 4 renumbers AML § 301(16) as added by Chapter 536 of the Laws
of 2008 as AML § 301(17) because there are two subdivisions 16, and
renumbers AML § 301(17) as AML § 301(18).

Section 5 amends AML § 303 to streamline the requirements for creation
of an agricultural district.

Section 6 amends AML § 303-a to streamline the requirements for review
of an agricultural district.

Section 7 adds a new AML § 303-c to establish the process for the
consolidation of an existing agricultural district or districts into a
district undergoing review under AML § 303-a.

Section 8 repeals AML § 304, eliminating the provisions for the
creation of agricultural districts for unique and irreplaceable lands.

Section 9 amends AML § 304-b(1) to make a technical amendment to
remove a reference to "planning" to more accurately reflect the
Department of Agriculture and Markets (DAM) Agricultural and Farmland
Protection Programs which go beyond planning grants.

Section 10 amends AML §§ 305(1)(d)(ii) and (iv) to increase the
penalty which a local assessing unit may impose if a landowner fails
to notify the assessor about conversion of agricultural land to
non-agricultural use up to $1,000 (from $500) and to increase the
minimum payment amount which may be imposed by a local assessing unit
for conversion to $500 (from $100).


Section 11 repeals AML § 305(1)(e) to conform to the repeal of AML
304 made by Section 5 of the bill. This section also re-letters
paragraph AML § 305(1)(f) as AML § 305(1)(e).

Section 12 repeals AML § 305(4)(b) to remove the requirement for
filing preliminary notices of intent to acquire a specified amount of
land from actively operated farms in an agricultural district, or
undertake or support certain specified development activities within
an agricultural district.

Section 13 amends AML §§ 301(4)(c), (d), (e) and (f) to remove
references to final notices of intent, and provide that notice of a
Commissioner's public hearing be posted on the Department's website
and sent by first class mail to affected municipalities, rather than
through publication. This section also re-letters theses paragraphs to
reflect the repeal of AML § 305(4)(b) made by Section 12 of the bill.

Section 14 re-letters AML § 305(4)(g),(h), and (h-1) to reflect the
re-lettering of AML § 305(4) made by Section 13 of the bill.

Section 15 repeals AML §§ 305-a(2), (3), and (4), in relation to
agricultural data statements, to reflect that this language is
included in a new AML § 305-b, added by Section 16 of the bill.

Section 16 renumbers AML § 305-b as AML § 305-c and adds a new
305-b, titled "Agricultural Data Statement" to adopt the language
repealed by Section 15 of the bill.

Section 17 amends AML §§ 306(2)(a)(iii) and (b)(iv) to increase the
penalty which a local assessing unit may impose if a landowner fails
to notify the assessor about conversion of agricultural land to
nonagricultural use up to $1,000

(from $500) and to increase the minimum payment amount which may be
imposed by a local assessing unit for conversion to $500 (from $100).

Section 18 amends AML § 307 to remove language granting authority to
promulgate regulations for consolidation of agricultural districts
because this language is included in a new AML § 303-c, as added by
Section 7 of the bill.

Section 19 amends AML § 308 (1)(a) to require the Commissioner of
Agriculture and Markets (Commissioner) to issue agricultural practice
opinions to any farm owner or operator only, rather than to "any
person."

Section 20 repeals AML § 308(4) to eliminate the requirement that the
Commissioner issue opinions on whether particular land uses are
agricultural in nature. This section also renumbers AML § 308(5) as
AML § 308(4).

Section 21 amend AML § 309(6) to provide that the Advisory Council on
Agriculture (ACA) shall meet as needed to complete council business,
eliminating the requirement that it meet at least four times a year.

Section 22 repeals AML § 309(8) which provides that the ACA shall
advise the Commissioner whether particular land uses are agricultural,


consistent with the repeal of AML § 308(4), as made by Section 20 of
the bill.

Section 23 amends Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) § 483(2) to expressly
provide that the term "structures and buildings" includes permanent
and impermanent structures, including, but not limited to metal,
string, or wood trellises and pergolas.

Section 24 provides the effective date.

Existing Law:

AML § 301 defines terms for AML Article 25-AA "Agricultural
Districts;" AML § 303 sets forth the process for the creation of
agricultural districts; AML § 303-a provides for review of
agricultural districts; AML § 304 authorizes the creation of
agricultural districts for Unique and Irreplaceable Lands; AML § 304-b
requires reporting of agricultural district data to the Governor and
the Legislature; AML § 305 (Agricultural Assessments), among other
things, sets forth various benefits for land in agricultural
districts; AML § 305(1) provides for a maximum penalty of $500 for
failing to notify an assessor about conversion of agricultural land to
a non-agricultural use and authorizes a minimum payment of $100 for
such conversion; AML § 305(1)(e) provides for State assistance to
localities for one-half of the tax loss that results from requests for
agricultural assessments in an agricultural district created under AML
§ 304; AML § 305(4) sets forth the requirements for filing preliminary
and final notices of intent with the Commissioner and the County
Agricultural and Farmland Protection Board; AML §§ 305-a (2), (3) and
(4) require Agricultural Data Statements; AML § 306(1) (Agricultural
Assessments - Lands Outside Agricultural Districts) provides for a
maximum penalty of $500 for failing to notify an assessor about
conversion of agricultural land to a non-agricultural use and
authorizes a minimum payment of $100 for such conversion; AML § 307
provides authority for regulations to implement AML Article 25-A; AML
§ 308(1)(a) (Right to Farm) states that the Commissioner shall issue
agricultural practice opinions to "any person;" AML § 308(4) requires
the Commissioner to issue opinions upon request form any person as to
whether particular land uses are agricultural in nature; AML § 309(6)
(Advisory Council on Agriculture-ACA) requires that the ACA hold at
least four meetings per year; and § 309(8) tasks the ACA with advising
the Commissioner in regards to whether particular land uses are
agricultural in nature.

RPTL § 483(2) sets forth various structures and buildings used by
farms that are exempt from the real property tax for a period of 10
years from their construction or reconstruction.

Prior Legislative History:

This is a new bill.

Statement in Support:

The Agricultural Districts Law, enacted in 1971, has been amended many
times to better protect farms and farmers, to facilitate the creation
of agricultural districts, and to streamline the establishment and


review process for county governments and DAM staff. This bill is
designed to further streamline the creation, review and consolidation
process, repeal certain provisions that have created unnecessary delay
or created inefficiencies, and better focus the statute to achieve the
goals of the original law - the protection of farms and farmers.

Farm Woodland and Agricultural Assessment

Under AML § 3014)(d), up to 50 acres of "farm woodland" per parcel is
eligible for an agricultural assessment. However, so long as the term
"farm woodland" is defined in AML § 301(3) as "...land used for the
production for sale of woodland products ..." some land in
agricultural production may not be eligible for agricultural
assessment. For example, timber and forest products are long-term
products that do not produce annual revenue; especially if the
woodland is being managed for saw timber production. Further, farm
woodland is often used by farms to provide woodland products (such as
posts and lumber for fencing and firewood for heating) for on-farm
use. Some assessors have denied farmers agricultural assessment if
they cannot show annual sales of woodland products. This bill would
correct this result by clarifying that actual sale of woodland
products is not necessary for land in use for agricultural purposes to
be eligible for agricultural assessment.

Enhanced Ease in Creation and Review of Agricultural Districts

This bill would remove impediments and inefficiencies in the creation
and review process. Notice provisions have been updated and improved,
substituting notification by posting on the web and mail notification
of affected counties for publication in newspapers (a less than
reliable method of notification). The proposed amendments to AML
303-eliminate the requirement for public hearings after the
Commissioner's certification of the agricultural district proposal.
(A public hearing is still required before the county acts to adopt or
reject the proposal as a plan.) Unrealistic time deadlines have

been eliminated. Participation of the county planning boards in the
creation of the agricultural districts would be eliminated,
reconciling AML § 303 with AML § 303-a, which removed the county
planning boards from the agricultural district review process, in
part, because the Agricultural and Farmland Protection Board (AFPB)
includes the county planning director.

As the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) has not been
participating in the establishment or review of agricultural
districts, the bill also removes the DEC from the process to enhance
efficiencies. In this regard, several years ago the Secretary of State
was removed from the district creation and review processes for lack
of participation.

The proposal designates an 8 year review period as no district created
since the law was adopted in 1971 has selected the 12 or 20 year
options.As of July 1, 2013, 95 of the 238 districts (approximately
40%) were not timely in conducting the 8-year reviews of districts
required by the AML. However, the 11 counties that have consolidated
multiple districts into a single, county-wide agricultural district
were all timely in the 8-year review process. These statistics


evidence a need to help counties streamline how they create, review
and consolidate agricultural districts, which these amendments seek to
address.

Increased Penalties

AML §§ 305(1) and § 306 (2) require landowners to notify the assessor
when land receiving an agricultural assessment is converted to a
non-agricultural use and authorizes penalties and minimal payments for
such conversions to be imposed on landowners who fail to notify the
assessor of a conversion. The penalties are established to ensure that
the assessor is made aware of a conversion so that conversion
payments, which compensate the locality for the prior benefits of
agricultural assessments received, may be calculated and levied on the
property. Many assessing units do not levy these payments or penalties
because the current statutory amounts are too small.  Increased
penalties and minimum payment amounts will encourage assessing units
to levy the payments and penalties and help ensure that landowners
comply with the law.

DAM Opinions

AML § 308(1) requires the Commissioner to issue agricultural practice
opinions to any person upon request. The purpose of the agricultural
practice opinion is to protect a farmer from a private nuisance cause
of action. When someone other than a farmer requests an opinion, DAM
cannot easily conduct a sound agricultural practice review. Often,
when agricultural practice opinions are sought by non-farmers, their
intended use is to challenge farm practices. DAM must contact the
farmer and obtain permission to access the property and otherwise have
the cooperation of the farmer to conduct a review and issue an
opinion. In light of the possible use of such an opinion, cooperation
of the farmer is often difficult to obtain. Notably, an agricultural
practice opinion has no binding effect other than in a private
nuisance lawsuit. In DAM's experience, however, such opinions are
sought by non-farmers for a wide range of disputes and matters
unrelated to private nuisance lawsuits.

AML § 308(4) requires the Commissioner to issue opinions as to whether
particular land uses are "agricultural in nature" upon request from
any person. These opinions, while informal and non-binding, are
problematic because non-farm neighbors, local governments, and others
sometimes use the opinions against a farmer to try to stop an
agricultural activity or otherwise affect the outcome of a proceeding
involving a farmer or farm interests.

Property Tax Exemptions for Farming Structures

The proposed amendment of RPTL § 483(2) would make it clear that
permanent and impermanent structures, including, but not limited to
metal, string, or wood trellises and pergolas can qualify for the 10
year property tax exemption for structures and buildings used
exclusively in the raising and production for sale of agricultural or
horticultural commodities.

Although an opinion of the former State Board of Equalization and
Assessment (Vol. 3- Opns of Counsel SBEA No. 19) determined that that


newly constructed vineyard trellises come within the meaning of
"structures and buildings" for purposes of RPTL § 483(2), a statutory
clarification that ensures consistent results is important for the
hops producers and other farmers that use impermanent structures for
production.

Budget Implications:

None.

Local Impact:

This bill would not impose any mandate on local governments. Municipal
governments should recognize cost savings over time from the
streamlining measures proposed in the bill.

Effective Date:

This bill would take effect immediately, except Section 5 of the bill
shall only apply to the creation of any agricultural district pursuant
to AML § 303 commenced after such effective date and Section 6 of the
bill shall only apply to the review of any agricultural district
pursuant to AML § 303-a commenced after the effective date.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S4851A

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the agriculture and markets law, in relation to
agricultural districts law improvements; and the real property tax
law, in relation to tax exemptions for certain structures on
agricultural and horticultural lands; and to repeal certain provisions
of the agriculture and markets law relating to agricultural districts

Purpose of the Bill:

The purpose of this bill is to amend the Agriculture and Markets Law
(AML) to streamline the process for the creation, review and
consolidation of agricultural districts; and repeal certain provisions
of the law to improve efficiency, clarity and farmer protections. The
bill also amends the Real Property Tax Law's (RPTL) property tax
exemption for structures and buildings used exclusively in the raising
and production for sale of agricultural or horticultural commodities
to expressly include permanent and impermanent structures and
buildings.

Summary of Provisions:

Section 1 of the bill amends AML § 16 to add a new subdivision 48 to
authorize the Department to develop, and update, guidance and other
information to assist local officials in creating, reviewing and
consolidating agricultural districts; and assist the commissioner of
taxation and finance to support training of assessors and any other
local government officials who have responsibility for agricultural
assessment and taxation.

Section 2 of the bill amends subdivision 3 of AML § 301 to clarify the
definition of "farm woodland" as land used for the production of
woodland products intended for sale.

Section 3 of the bill amends subdivision 11 of AML § 301, the
definition of "farm operation," to the extent of renumbering of
subdivisions "16" and "17" as subdivisions "17" and "18" and amends
subdivision 12 of AML § 301, the definition of "agricultural data
statement," to reflect the inclusion of the agricultural data
statement provisions in the new § 305-b.

Section 4 of the bill renumbers subdivision "16" of AML § 301 as
subdivision "17".

Section 5 of the bill renumbers subdivision "17" of AML § 301 as
subdivision "18".

Section 6 amends AML § 303: (1) streamlining the process by removing
the requirement of (a) county planning board review; (b) a DEC
determination on a plan's consistency with environmental plans,
policies and objectives; and (c) a public hearing; (2) requiring
notice of the proposed district by posting on the county's website, in
addition to the currently required newspaper publication, coupled with
mail notice to affected municipalities, (3) modifying time periods so


as to conform to actual practice, and (4) establishing the district
upon the certification of the Commissioner

Section 7 amends AML § 303-a (1) requiring the review of the
agricultural district eight years after its creation and every eight
years thereafter, (2) providing for the same notice provisions for the
periodic review and public hearing as required for the initial plan
proposal; (3) setting a 45-day deadline for the agricultural and
farmland protection board's report; (4) granting the county
legislative body the power to adopt any modification of the review
plan it deems appropriate, (5) requiring the county legislative body
to complete the review process within a year of the district's
anniversary date, unless, upon the county legislature's request to the
commissioner and for good cause, the commissioner grants an extension
for up to six months; and (6) eliminating the DEC's review of the
district's continuation

Section 8 amends the AML by adding a new § 303-c to establish the
process for the consolidation of an existing agricultural district
with one undergoing review under Section 303-a.

Section 9 repeals AML § 304, eliminating the provisions for the
creation of agricultural districts for unique and irreplaceable lands.

Section 10 amends subdivision 1 of AML § 304-b to make a technical
correction to remove a reference to "planning" to more accurately
reflect the Department of Agriculture and Markets (Department)
Agricultural and Farmland Protection Programs which go beyond planning
grants.

Section 11 amends subparagraphs (ii) and (vi) of AML § 305(1) (d) to
increase the penalty which a local assessing unit may impose if a
landowner fails to notify the assessor about conversion of
agricultural land to a non-agricultural use to $1,000 (from $500) and
to increase the minimum payment amount which may be imposed by a local
assessing unit for conversion to $500 (from $100.

Section 12 would repeal AML § 305(1) (e), which authorizes state
assistance for districts created for unique and irreplaceable lands
under AML § 304, because those districts would no longer be authorized
due to the repeal of AML§ 304 under Section 5 of the bill This section
also re-letters paragraph "f' as paragraph "e".

Section 13 would repeal AML § 305(4) (b) to remove the requirement for
filing preliminary notices of intent to acquire specified amount of
land from actively operated farms in the agricultural district, or
undertake or support certain specified development activities within
an agricultural district.

Section 14 amends paragraphs "c", "d", "e" and "f" of subdivision "4"
of AML § 305 by relettering them as paragraphs "b", "c", "d" and "e";
removing references to final notices of intent; and providing that
notice of a commissioner's public hearing be posted on the
Department's website and sent by first class mail to affected
municipalities, rather than through publication.


Section 15 reletters paragraphs "g", "h" and "h-1" of subdivision "4"
of AML § 305 as paragraphs "f", "g" and "h".

Section 16 repeals subdivisions "2", "3" and "4" of AML § 305-a, in
relation to agricultural data statements, as Section "16" of the bill
adds this language in a new AML § 305-b.

Section 17 renumbers AML § 305-b as § 305-c and adds a new § 305-b,
titled "Agricultural Data Statement" to adopt the language repealed in
Section 15 of the bill.

Section 18 of the bill would amend subparagraph "iii" of paragraph "a"
and subparagraph "iv" of paragraph "b" of AML § 306(2) to increase the
penalty which a local assessing unit may impose if a landowner fails
to notify the assessor about conversion of agricultural land to a
non-agricultural use to $1,000 (from $500) and to increase the minimum
payment amount which may be imposed by a local assessing unit for
conversion to $500 (from $100).

Section 19 of the bill would amend AML § 307 to remove language
granting authority to promulgate regulations for consolidation of
agricultural districts because Section 7 of the bill (new AML § 303-c)
establishes a process for the consolidation of existing agricultural
districts.

Section 20 of the bill would amend AML § 309(6) to provide that the
Advisory Council on Agriculture (ACA) shall meet at least one time per
year.

Section 21 of the bill would amend Real Property Tax Law (RPTL)
483(2) to expressly provide that the term "structures and buildings"
includes permanent and impermanent structures, including trellises and
pergolas made of metal, string or wood.

Section 22 provides for an immediate effective date, except Section 6
shall only apply to the creation of any agricultural district pursuant
to AML § 303 commenced after such effective date and Section 7 shall
only apply to the review of any agricultural district pursuant to AML
§ 303-a commenced after the effective date.

Existing Law:

AML § 16 provides for various general powers of the Department.

AML § 301 defines terms for AML Article 25-AA, Agricultural Districts.

AML § 303 sets forth the process for Creation of Agricultural
Districts.

AML § 303-a provides for Review of Agricultural Districts.

AML § 304 authorizes the Creation of Agricultural Districts for Unique
and Irreplaceable Lands.

AML § 304-b requires reporting of agricultural district data to the
Governor and the Legislature.


AML § 305 (Agricultural Assessments), among other things, sets forth
various benefits for land in agricultural districts.

Subdivision 1 of AML § 305 provides for a maximum penalty of $500 for
failing to notify an assessor about conversion of agricultural land to
a non-agricultural use and authorizes a minimum payment of $100 for
such conversion.

Paragraph e of subdivision 1 of AML § 305 provides for State
assistance to localities for one-half of the tax loss that results
from requests for agricultural assessments in agricultural district
created under AML § 304.

Subdivision 4 of AML § 305 sets forth the requirements for filing
preliminary and final notices of intent with the Commissioner and the
County Agricultural and Farmland Protection Board.

Subdivisions 2, 3 and 4 of AML § 305-a require Agricultural Data
Statements.

Subdivision 1 of AML § 306 (Agricultural Assessments - Lands Outside
Agricultural Districts) provides for a maximum penalty of $500 for
failing to notify an assessor about conversion of agricultural land to
a non-agricultural use and authorizes a minimum payment of $100 for
such conversion.

AML § 307 provides authority for regulations to implement AML Article
25-AA, Agricultural Districts.

Subdivision 6 of AML § 309 (Advisory Council on Agriculture ACA)
requires that the ACA hold at least four meetings per year.

Subdivision 2 of RPTL § 483 sets forth various structures and
buildings used by farms that are exempt from the real property tax for
a period of 10 years from their construction or reconstruction.

Prior Legislative History:

This proposal was not approved for introduction in 2014.

Statement in Support:

The Agricultural Districts Law, enacted in 1971, has been amended many
times to: (a) better protect farms and farmers; (b) facilitate the
creation of agricultural districts: and (c) streamline the
establishment and review process for county governments and Department
staff. This bill is designed to streamline the creation, review and
consolidation process and to repeal certain provisions that have
created unnecessary delay or created inefficiencies.

Assistance to Counties with the Creation, Review and Consolidation of
Agricultural Districts; and Support for Agricultural Assessment
Training of Assessors

The proposed addition of subdivision 48 to AML § 16 acknowledges the
assistance that the Department currently provides to counties and
county agricultural and farmland protection boards with the


agricultural districts program as part of Department administration of
AML Article 25-AA. The Department often receives calls from local
assessors and the public concerning the agricultural assessment
program. The Department has been charged by the NYS Advisory Council
on Agriculture to participate in the agricultural assessment program,
coordinate with the Department of Taxation and Finance as needed, and
participate in the training of local government officials and the
public on this very important program. While the Department is not
statutorily required to provide such assistance, the Department makes
every effort to further the understanding of these critical provisions
of Article 25-AA, which help ensure that land stays in agricultural
production and that farm operations continue to be viable The proposed
amendment recognizes this role.

Farm Woodland and Agricultural Assessment

Under AML § 301(4) (d), up to 50 acres of "farm woodland" per parcel
is eligible for an agricultural assessment. However, so long as the
term "farm woodland" is defined in AML § 301(3) as "... land used for
the production for sale of woodland products ..." some land in
agricultural production may not be eligible for agricultural
assessment. For example, timber and forest products are long-term
products that do not produce annual revenue; especially if the
woodland is being managed for saw timber production. Further, farm
woodland is often used by farms to provide woodland products (such as
posts and lumber for fencing and firewood for heating) for on-farm
use.

Some assessors have denied farmers an agricultural assessment if they
cannot show annual sales of woodland products. This proposed amendment
would clarify that land used for the production of woodland products
intended for sale is eligible for agricultural assessment.

Enhanced Ease in Creation and Review of Agricultural Districts

The proposed amendments remove impediments and inefficiencies in the
creation and review process. Notice provisions have been updated to
include notification by posting on the web in addition to mail
notification of affected municipalities. The proposed amendments to
AML § 303-eliminate the requirement for public hearings after the
Commissioner's certification of the agricultural district proposal (A
public hearing is still required before the county acts to adopt or
reject the proposal as a plan.) Unrealistic time deadlines have been
eliminated.

County planning boards would no longer have to provide a report as
part of the process for the creation of agricultural districts The
boards would still be consulted as part of the process, however.

As the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) has not been
participating in the establishment or review of agricultural
districts, the proposal removes the DEC from the process to enhance
efficiencies In this regard, several years ago the Secretary of State
was removed from the district creation and review processes for lack
of participation.


The proposal designates an 8-year review period as no district created
since the law was adopted in 1971 has selected the 12-or 20-year
options.

As of July 1, 2013, 95 of the 238 districts (approximately 40%) were
not timely in conducting the 8-year reviews of districts required by
the AML. However, the 11 counties that have consolidated multiple
districts into a single, county-wide agricultural district were all
timely in the 8-year review process. These statistics evidence a need
to help counties streamline how they create, review and consolidate
agricultural districts, which these amendments seek to address.

Increased Penalties

AML §§ 305(1) and § 306 (2) require landowners to notify the assessor
when land receiving an agricultural assessment is converted to a
non-agricultural use and authorizes penalties and minimal payments for
such conversions to be imposed on landowners who fail to notify the
assessor of a conversion The penalties are established to ensure that
the assessor is made aware of a conversion so that conversion
payments, which compensate the locality for the prior benefits of
agricultural assessments received, may be calculated and levied on the
property.

Many assessing units do not levy these payments or penalties because
the current statutory amounts are too small. Increased penalties and
minimum payment amounts will encourage assessing units to levy the
payments and penalties and help ensure that landowners comply with the
law.

Property Tax Exemptions for Farming Structures

The proposed amendment of RPTL § 483(2) would make it clear that
permanent and impermanent structures, including metal, string, or wood
trellises and pergolas can qualify for the provisions a 10-year
property tax exemption for structures and buildings used exclusively
in the raising and production for sale of agricultural or
horticultural commodities.

Although an opinion of the former State Board of Equalization and
Assessment (Vol 3- Opns of Counsel SBEA No. 19) determined that that
newly constructed vineyard trellises come within the meaning of
"structures and buildings" for purposes of RPTL § 483(2), a statutory
clarification that ensures consistent results is important for the
hops producers and other farmers that use impermanent structures for
production.

Budget Implications:

None.

Local Impact:

This bill would not impose a mandate on a county, city, town, village,
school district or special district.


The resulting changes would provide no additional costs to municipal
governments. The changes to the Agricultural Districts Law streamline
the processes for creation, review and consolidation of agricultural
districts; thereby responding to local entities surveyed by the
Department. Thus, municipal governments should recognize cost savings
over time from these modifications.

Effective Date:

The amendments take effect upon enactment, except Section 5 shall only
apply to the creation of any agricultural district pursuant to AML
303 commenced after such effective date and Section 6 shall only apply
to the review of any agricultural district pursuant to AML § 303-a
commenced after the effective date.
